en: The Sūtra on the Visualization of the Maṇḍala for Purifying All Evil Destinies Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
I take refuge in the King who purifies all evil realms, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
With a single-minded mind, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas, who taught the maṇḍala that extinguishes the evil realms;
I do so now for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Regarding the fundamental Great Teaching spoken by the Tathāgata,
which expounds the method of the Great Maṇḍala for purifying all evil destinies through meditative visualization:
when the Ācārya wishes to perform the rite, [he should proceed as follows].
First, having chosen a quiet place and sat down with a settled mind,
once the realization that phenomena are devoid of self has become manifest before you,
you should then visualize a great lotus flower emerging from the nape of your own neck.
Upon the lotus, the syllable *A* appears.
One should further visualize that the syllable *A* transforms into a moon disc,
and then visualize that the moon disc transforms into the syllable *HŪṂ*.
The syllable HŪṂ transforms into a five-pronged vajra.
One should further visualize this vajra moving onto the tongue;
only then is it called the "vajra tongue."
From this point forward, one may perform the recitation with mastery.
Next, one should visualize the syllable *A* within both hands;
the syllable *A* transforms into a lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*).
The lunar disc transforms into the syllable HŪṂ.
The syllable HŪṂ transforms into a white five-pronged vajra.
Having thus visualized it until it appears clearly before one:
Only then is one named "Firm Vajrapāṇi.
Subsequently, one may employ this hand to bind all mudrās and perform protection by means of the Vajrapravarabha rite.
One constructs the Vajradhātu using the *vajra-śikhara-kāra* and so forth;
by surrounding it with vajras, one thus establishes the boundary to benefit sentient beings.
Furthermore, one should visualize space as likewise establishing the boundary.
In the center, a maṇḍala was formed.
Within the maṇḍala were countless Buddha-bodies, the size of mustard seeds,
with all their marks and signs of excellence perfectly distinct and majestic.
Then the ācārya should visualize offering scented ointments, incense, named flowers,
and lamps, up to various kinds of most excellent food and drink;
he should further visualize these outside the space-maṇḍala.
Furthermore, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, mahoragas, bhūtas, piśācas, piśācīs,
and others all came to rejoice and likewise received offerings.
Having performed the offerings in this manner,
one should take these merits and dedicate them toward repentance and the aspiration for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, one should praise the virtues of the Buddha with sublime words.
Then he spoke in verse:
My Buddha, the Most Honored One, The Great Teacher of gods and humans,
Excellent is it that by the power of the Dharma, He is able to purify all evil realms.
Sentient beings were freed from the evil realms; practicing the path, they realized Bodhi.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others joined their palms in homage to the Buddha.
Having each paid obeisance to the Buddha, they vanished from sight and were no longer seen.
Having thus visualized each part clearly until accomplishment is attained,
one next visualizes a moon disc within the heart, and upon that moon disc, one visualizes a maṇḍala.
Once it has been manifested before one,
one then further visualizes the maṇḍala in the sky until it likewise appears clearly.
Then, having formed the Vajrāṅkuśa mudrā, draw [the deity] into the heart.
Visualize that the two maṇḍalas merge into one.
Furthermore, form the mudrā and remain established therein.
This immediately constitutes the ultimate corresponding maṇḍala.
Within this maṇḍala, one should visualize oneself as Śākyamuni Buddha.
Within the heart of the Buddha, a full moon appears again;
within that moon, one should visualize the subtle mantra of the deity named "Purifier of All Evils."
As soon as one brings this wondrous mantra to mind,
in an instant it emits great radiance that universally illumines the realms of all sentient beings.
Down to the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals,
whatever sentient beings are illuminated by that light shall have their karmic offenses completely extinguished, leaving nothing behind, through the power of that light.
Furthermore, one visualizes that the light has extinguished the evil destinies,
and then summons those sentient beings to enter the corresponding maṇḍala.
At that time, the ācārya orally recites the subtle mantra of empowerment.
One bestows the pure water of the Dharma upon their crowns,
causing all sentient beings to become sons of the Buddha.
Furthermore, one should visualize making offerings with the most sublime and excellent implements to them universally.
The ācārya, holding the bell and the vajra,
recites this verse of praise before the maṇḍala:
"I prostrate to the Lion of the Śākyas, who excellently turns the sublime Wheel of Dharma."
Able to extinguish all evil destinies within the three realms,
I bow my head to the Vajra-peak. You have expounded the principle of the Dharma-realm mantra,
the ultimate truth, for the benefit of all sentient beings.
I prostrate to the crown of Ratnasambhava, who impartially observes the realm of sentient beings;
to all beings throughout the three worlds, he bestows empowerment.
I prostrate to the crown of Padmanarteshvara, whose self-nature is wondrous discernment.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, you let fall the nectar rain of the Dharma;

I bow my head to the crown of your *karma*-seal. You who perform through your own nature, you who receive and accomplish various deeds, you who pacify the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings.

I prostrate to the Radiant Summit, which can universally illuminate the sentient beings within the evil realms of the triple world; I prostrate to the Jewel Banner Summit, which is well able to provide rescue and protection,
and which holds the wish-fulfilling jewel banner.
Bestowing material gifts upon all sentient beings, you are able to fulfill all their aspirations;
I bow my head to the Beneficial Uṣṇīṣa, who can sever all afflictions,
subdue the armies of the four Māras, and bring about the perfect awakening of all beings.
I prostrate to the White Parasol, whose body endowed with all marks pervades the three realms; to the sole Dharma-King,
who sports with garlands and song and dance, and with incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments.
I constantly attend upon and behold the Tathāgata; now, with utmost sincerity, I prostrate to the worthy sages who guard the gates.
To the Hook, the Noose, the Chain, and the Bell, each abiding in their respective positions, I now prostrate with utmost sincerity.
I prostrate to the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas of the ten stages, from the Stage of Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma; now, with utmost sincerity,
I prostrate to Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, and Maheśvara.
The sun, moon, fire, and wind, along with the rākṣasas, bhūtas, and others,
are all able to protect the ten directions; having single-mindedly bowed my head and offered praise, I [proceed].
Furthermore, one should visualize that the three realms are entirely empty.
Between the limits of wind and water, a golden wheel is manifested.
Upon this golden wheel, one should visualize the appearance of the syllable *Svaṃ*.
The character *Song* (宋) transforms into Mount Sumeru,
composed of the four jewels, vast and expansive on all four sides.
Upon that mountain, one should visualize the appearance of the syllable *ḍaṅga*.
It transformed into a great maṇḍala named Purifying All Evil Destinies.
This maṇḍala had four sides and four gates,
with a pavilion above each gate.
It is bounded by four cords.
At its four gates and four corners, there are various adornments of vajra-jewels.
Furthermore, necklaces and precious bells made of various jewels are suspended everywhere.
Surrounded on all four sides by jeweled banners and canopies,
one should visualize an eight-spoked wheel within the maṇḍala;
at the center of the wheel is a lotus flower, and within the flower is a lion throne made of jewels.
Upon the seat is a moon disc.
Within the moon disc is Śākyamuni Buddha, who,
through great compassion, wisdom, and skillful means, [manifests].
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he manifested the form of a mantra. The mantra is:
Oṃ muni muni mahāmune svāhā. At that time, the ācārya again entered samādhi.
Named "Remover of Obstructions Purifying All Evil Destinies," he emerged from samādhi,
recited the aforementioned King of Mantras, and bound the Dharma-Wheel mudrā.
Form the mudrā with both hands by making vajra-fists,
then opening them sequentially from the thumb and ring finger;
while reciting the mantra, one should bind the seal.
He is able to sever the karma of saṃsāra for all sentient beings. Furthermore, he spoke a verse by way of simile:
"Just as when a swarm of bees gathers nectar from a lotus flower, If they encounter night and the flower closes, they cannot escape;
But at dawn, when the sun rises and the flower opens, Those bees that were gathering nectar finally gain their release."
The saṃsāra of sentient beings is likewise; they constantly suffer the shackles of the three realms of existence.
Śākyasiṃha, the Great Compassionate One, releases them from their bonds and brings them to liberation.
Having spoken this analogy, the Ācārya said:
Again, visualize the moon disc appearing before you within the heart center.
Then, begin the recitation of the mantras starting from the *Vajra-mahā-uṣṇīṣa* up to the *Vajrāṅkuśa*, as follows:
Oṃ namo sarvatathāgatapariśuddhadharmanairātmyāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya tadyathā śodhani viśodhani viśodhani sarvavaraṇaviśodhani svāhā. Having recited this mantra:
Furthermore, the mantra is spoken as follows:
Oṃ vajra hūṃ phaṭ. When reciting this mantra, one should visualize five-colored light rays arising from the heart center.
Emerging from the mouth together with the mantra,
it universally illumines all worlds,
causing all the sufferings and afflictions of the sentient beings therein to be completely extinguished.
The light and the mantra merge into one.
That light returns and re-enters the fundamental mind.
Once more, from within the mind, there emerges the Tathāgata of the Great Vajra Uṣṇīṣa.
He is fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
His body is white in color, blazing with intense radiance,
and his hands form the earth-touching mudrā.
One should settle [the deity] upon the eastern spoke of the maṇḍala wheel.
Then, recite the mantra: Oṃ ratna-maṇḍalam. While reciting this mantra:
As before, light issues from the mouth and, together with the mantra,
universally illuminates all worlds;
having thus extinguished the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings.
He returns once more to his original mind. From within that mind,
there again emanates the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhavottama,
his body a deep blue color, complete with the primary and secondary marks of perfection, and blazing with intense radiance.
Forming the mudrā of granting boons with his hands,
he bestows empowerment upon all sentient beings of the three realms;
he is established in the position of the southern spoke of the maṇḍala wheel.
Again, recite the mantra:
Oṃ padmodbhava-hṛdaya. When reciting this mantra, as before, light issues forth from the mouth together with the mantra.
It universally illumines all worlds within the three realms;
having extinguished the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings,
it returns once more to enter the fundamental mind.
Furthermore, he emanated the Tathāgata Padmottama,
whose body was red in color, endowed with the primary and secondary marks, and blazing with intense radiance;
his hands formed the mudrā of meditative concentration.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings within the three realms,
establish them in the position of the western spoke of the maṇḍala wheel.
Then, recite the mantra as follows:
Oṃ viśvottama. When reciting this mantra,
as before, light issues from the mouth and, together with the mantra,
illuminates all the worlds of the three realms.
Having extinguished the suffering and afflictions of sentient beings,
he returns to his original mind and manifests the Karmamukuṭa Tathāgata.
His body is green, endowed with the primary and secondary marks of perfection, and blazing with intense radiance.
His hands form the mudrā of granting fearlessness,
capable of accomplishing all manner of activities.
Having rescued sentient beings and liberated them from saṃsāra,
he is established in the position of the northern spoke of the maṇḍala wheel.
Next, the syllable Oṃ (𑆃) emerges from the visualization of the mind.
From the syllable Oṃ, there arises the Tathāgata Śikhin,
his body white with a reddish tint, endowed with all the marks and signs of perfection;
his blazing radiance intensely illuminates the three realms.
Holding a solar disc in his right hand and placing his left hand at his waist,
he is stationed upon the spoke in the southeast corner of the maṇḍala wheel.
Furthermore, from the mind, the syllable HŪṂ emerges.
From the syllable HŪṂ, the Tathāgata Ratnaketūrdhva is born,
his body dark red in color, endowed with the primary and secondary marks of perfection,
and blazing with intense radiance that illuminates the three realms.
Holding a wish-fulfilling jewel banner (*cintāmaṇi-dhvaja*) in his hand,
he is able to purify the defilements of greed and envy in sentient beings;
place him on the spoke-position at the southwest corner of the maṇḍala wheel.
Furthermore, from the mind’s thought, the syllable *ṬI* emerges.
From the syllable *ṬI*, there arises the Tathāgata Śrī-Uṣṇīṣa,
whose body is the color of space.
Endowed with the primary and secondary marks, his radiant flames blaze intensely,
illuminating the three realms to benefit sentient beings;
his right hand holds a sword and his left hand holds a scripture.
Rest in the spoke-position at the northwest corner of the maṇḍala wheel.
Next, from the mental visualization, the syllable *kṛiṃ* emerges;
from the syllable *kṛiṃ*, the Tathāgata Śvetacchatraśikhara is born.
His body is pure white, endowed with the primary and secondary marks of perfection;
his blazing radiance illuminates the three realms,
and he holds a white parasol in his hand.
In the spoke-position at the northeast corner of the maṇḍala wheel,
all the Tathāgatas are seated upon lotus thrones made of various jewels, according to the arrangement of these wheel spokes.
Furthermore, from the mind-visualization, there emerges the mantra *HŪṂ TRAṂ HRĪḤ ĀḤ*.
From this mantra, the four attendant Bodhisattvas are born.
Their bodily color, appearance, and hand gestures are all established according to the ritual rules,
seated upon moon-discs atop lotuses at the four corners outside the wheel.
Furthermore, from the mind’s thought, there emerge the eight bodhisattvas— Gandha, Puṣpa, Dīpa, Upalepana, Lāsya, Mālya, Gīta,
and Nṛtya— and others. Outside the maṇḍala wheel,
they each sit in succession upon lotus seats according to their respective original positions.
Having thus established [the deity], one next recites the mantra:
Oṃ sarvasaṃskārapariśuddhadharmate gaganasamudgate mahānaya parivāri svāhā. While reciting this mantra:
Furthermore, one should visualize the emergence of the sixteen great bodhisattvas, such as Maitreya and others;
these bodhisattvas are positioned at the four sides of the maṇḍala.
Each occupies four positions.
Beginning from the eastern gate of the maṇḍala,
first install Maitreya Bodhisattva.
His body is yellow in color, with blazing and intense flames;
his right hand holds a branch of a nāga-flower tree, and his left hand holds a kamaṇḍalu;
he sits in the full lotus posture upon a moon disc atop a lotus flower.
The second position is occupied by Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin.
His body is yellow in color;
his right hand holds a lotus flower, and his left hand rests at his waist.
He sits in the full lotus posture upon a lotus flower.
In the third position is established the Bodhisattva Sarvapāpavinashana,
whose body is white and ablaze with intense radiance.
Holding a hook in his right hand and a kamaṇḍalu in his left,
he sits in the vajraparyaṅka posture upon a moon disc atop a lotus.
In the fourth position is established the Bodhisattva Sarvāśokāndhakāravidhvaṃsana.
The body is yellowish-white in color, with blazing flames of light.
The right hand holds a jeweled staff, while the left hand forms a fist resting at the side of the waist.
He sits in the full-lotus posture upon a moon disc atop a lotus flower.
Furthermore, at the southern gate of the maṇḍala, four bodhisattvas are installed.
In the first position is installed Gandhahastin Bodhisattva;
his body is white and green, with blazing, intense flames.
The right hand holds a fragrant elephant, and the left hand rests at the side of the waist.
In the second position is established the Bodhisattva Vīra,
whose body is the color of white crystal and moonlight.
The right hand holds a sword and the left hand is formed into a fist resting at the side of the waist.
In the third position is placed the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha,
whose body is the color of space or a pale yellow-white.
In his right hand he holds a lotus flower upon which is the Treasury of the Sublime Dharma;
his left hand rests at his hip, symbolizing the ability to sustain the nature of space.
In the fourth position is established the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu.
The body is a great blue color.
The right hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel banner (cintāmaṇidhvaja).
The left hand forms a fist placed at the side of the waist.
These four bodhisattvas all sit cross-legged upon lotus flowers.
Furthermore, at the western gate of the maṇḍala, one should place four bodhisattvas;
in the first position, one places the bodhisattva Amṛtaprabha.
The body is like the color of the moon;
the right hand holds an amṛta flask,
and the left hand forms a fist resting at the side of the waist.
The second is the Bodhisattva Candraprabha.
His body is white in color,
and his right hand holds a blossoming lotus flower.
Upon the flower is a moon.
The left hand forms a fist resting at the side of the waist.
In the third position is the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla.
The body is reddish-white in color.
The right hand holds a jewel of blazing radiance;
the left hand forms a fist placed at the side of the waist.
In the fourth position is the Bodhisattva Jvalanaprabha.
His body is red in color,
and his two hands hold a vajra-paraśu.
These four bodhisattvas all sit in the full-lotus posture upon lotus-moon seats.
Furthermore, four bodhisattvas are to be placed at the northern gate of the maṇḍala.
In the first position is established the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, his body blue-white in color.
The right hand holds an utpala flower,
upon which is a vajra;
the left hand rests against the side of the waist.
The second is the Bodhisattva Anantamati,
whose body is like the color of the kumuda flower or the hue of the moon.
With both hands he holds a vessel of *jñāna-argha* (wisdom-offering water) to subdue all sentient beings.
The third is the Bodhisattva Anantaprabha (Infinite Light),
light green in color.
His right hand holds a lotus flower upon which rests a jewel-treasury.
The left hand forms a fist placed at the side of the waist.
In the fourth position is the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, his body yellow in color;
his right hand holds a branch of a jewel tree.
The left hand forms a fist and rests at the side of the waist.
These four bodhisattvas all sit in the full-lotus posture upon moon discs atop lotuses.
These are the sixteen great bodhisattvas.
Possessing great compassion, they are able to benefit sentient beings.
Furthermore, one should visualize the Bodhisattvas of the Four Protective Gates.
First, visualize the syllable *jaṃ*.
He is born from the body of the Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśa,
with a complexion like the kumuda flower or the color of the moon,
and is stationed at the eastern gate of the maṇḍala.
Next, visualize the syllable HŪṂ,
from which arises the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa,
whose body is yellow in color.
Holding a vajra-noose, he is stationed at the southern gate of the maṇḍala.
Next, one should visualize the syllable *Jā* (𑖧),
from which arises the Bodhisattva Vajraśṛṅkhalā.
Her body is red in color;
she holds a vajra-chain in her hand and is stationed at the western gate of the maṇḍala.
Next, visualize the syllable *Hūḥ*.
From it arises the Bodhisattva Vajraghaṇṭā,
whose body is the color of crystal.
Holding vajra bells,
they are stationed at the northern gate of the maṇḍala.
These four bodhisattvas, endowed with great compassion, all sit in the lotus posture upon moon discs atop lotuses.
This method of visualization is called the Samādhi of the Supreme Maṇḍala King, and is also called the Samādhi of the Karma King;
it brings the Lion of the Śākyas into manifest presence.
Abiding in all maṇḍalas to purify the evil destinies, he perceives sentient beings dwelling amidst manifold sufferings;
thus, by means of the primordial dharma, he explains them through differentiation.
Furthermore, he expounds the mudrās, mantras, and ritual procedures.
When one wishes to perform ritual acts by forming mudrās,
first recite this mantra:
Oṃ namo sarva-nirgatibhyaḥ pariśuddha-jñānāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya tadyathā | oṃ śodhani śodhani sarvapāpaviśodhani ṭiṭṭi svāhā || This is the Samādhi-mudrā of Śākyasiṃha.
Form the gesture of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-mudrā*) with both hands and visualize within the mind that it is truly accomplished as the seal.
The Vajroṣṇīṣa seal is also called the Vajra-dṛḍha seal.
With both hands, tightly form the vajra-bind (*vajrabandha*).
Form the seal by joining the tips of the middle fingers.
This is the Vajraprabha-uṣṇīṣa seal.
Without changing the previous seal, form the shape of a jewel with the two middle fingers.
Furthermore, it is transformed into the shape of a lotus;
as before, it is again like the form of a vajra;
the remaining fingers are like blazing light.
Furthermore, it is modified into the method for forming the mudrā with palms joined.
The mudrā does not change its previous form;
however, the two ring fingers and little fingers are raised and held upright.
Form the shape of a lotus with the two index fingers;
extend the two middle fingers like a vajra-ardhajara;
and place the vajra at the heart.
Furthermore, visualize a lotus and moon emerging from the neck; imagine the seal upon the moon, thereby forming the seal.
When performing this ritual seal, recite the aforementioned mantra while employing it together.
The Dharmacakra-mudrā is the seal of Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Bhūmisparśa-mudrā, the Varada-mudrā, the Dhyāna-mudrā, and the Abhaya-mudrā—
these four seals are to be employed according to the sequence of the ritual.
The mudrā of the Buddha-Usnīṣa of Radiant Light is also called the Samādhi Mudrā.
With the right hand, form the gesture of holding a staff and place it at the heart;
with the left hand, form the gesture of holding a sword.
Furthermore, change the position so that the index finger of the left hand is held upright and the index finger of the right hand is extended straight;
then, join the two hands together like a parasol to form the mudrā.
Previously, each mantra was used in conjunction with its respective mudrā;
now, regarding the Great Bodhi Mudrā,
one should rely upon the visualization of Vajrasattva and the fundamental teachings.
The eight bodhisattvas of incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, play, garlands, song, and dance,
as well as the four gate-guarding bodhisattvas,
each employ their respective mudrās according to the ritual prescriptions.
Furthermore, regarding the mudrās of the sixteen great bodhisattvas:
the mudrā of Maitreya Bodhisattva is formed by joining the two hands in the gesture of the vajra-fist.
Straighten the two index fingers and slightly bend the middle fingers as if holding a flower to form the mudrā;
this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin.
Form a fist with the left hand and place it at the side of the waist.
Extend the index and middle fingers of the right hand to form the shape of an eye; this constitutes the mudrā.
The mudrā of the Bodhisattva Sarvapāpaviśodhana:
Form vajra-fists with both hands;
extend the two index fingers and slightly bend them like hooks to form the seal.
The mudrā of the Bodhisattva Destroyer of All Darkness of Sorrow:
Form a fist with the left hand and place it at the side of the waist;
with the right hand, form the mudrā in the gesture of holding a precious staff.
The mudrā of the Bodhisattva Gandhahasti: form a fist with the left hand and place it at the navel;
the right hand forms the mudrā in the gesture of holding a lotus flower.
This is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Parākrama.
Form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it at the side of the waist;
with the right hand, form the mudrā in the gesture of holding a sword.
This is the mudrā of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva.
Form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it upon the heart;
form a vajra-fist with the right hand as well,
and rotate it clockwise in the space before you to form the mudrā.
The mudrā of the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu:
Form vajra-fists with both hands;
then, change the right hand into the gesture of holding a banner to form the seal.
The mudrā of the Bodhisattva Amṛtaprabha:
form the mudrā with both hands in the gesture of holding an *argha* vessel.
The mudrā of the Bodhisattva Candraprabha.
Form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it upon the thigh;
likewise form a vajra-fist with the right hand and place it against the side of the torso.
Then, change the position and extend the right fist.
Interlace the thumbs and little fingers so that they form a lunar disc;
this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla.
Place both hands facing each other at the heart;
forming the shape of a blossoming lotus constitutes the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Blazing Radiance (Jvalanaprabha).
Forming vajra-fists with both hands,
then changing them into the armor gesture placed at the chest constitutes the mudrā of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva.
Form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it at the side of the waist;
likewise form a vajra-fist with the right hand and place it upon the heart.
Then, extend the middle finger of the right hand upward to form the mudrā.
The mudrā of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:
Form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it upon the heart;
form the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*) with the right hand to constitute the seal.
The mudrā of the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa:
Form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it at the navel;
form the gesture of snapping the fingers with the right hand to complete the mudrā.
The mudrā of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva:
Form a vajra-fist with the left hand and place it at the side of the waist;
form a fist with the right hand like a jewel to constitute the seal.
All these mudrās are to be used together with the aforementioned mantras.
Alternatively, one may use the insignia (cihna); if no insignia is available, use the karma-mudrā.
One should understand the characteristics of these great mudrās in this manner.
Furthermore, when first entering the maṇḍala,
one should first form the vajra-mudrā with both hands and recite the mantra to purify all sins within the body.
The mantra is:
Oṃ sarvavidbuddha-vajrā-tiṣṭhāna-samaye hūṃ. When reciting this mantra:
Seal the heart, neck, two eyes, space between the eyebrows, nose, ears, waist, knees, calves, both feet,
and the private parts with the mudrā to provide protection.
Then, reciting the mantra, hook out all karmic offenses within the body.
The mantra is:
Oṃ śodhani sarvapāpāni hūṃ. Recite this again to purify all sins within the body.
The mantra is:
Oṃ sarvavid-pāpaviśodhani hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this again to purify all evil destinies.
The mantra is:
Oṃ sarvavid tṛt tṛt haḥ. The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Visualization of the Maṇḍala for Purifying All Evil Destinies Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmabhadra, Subject of the Imperial Court, Preliminary Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments and Grand Master of Illuminating Teaching, under Imperial Decree. The mantra of Śākyamuni Buddha is as follows:
Oṃ sarvavid huṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the Great Vajra Uṣṇīṣa: Oṃ sarvavighnaviśodhani muḥ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ sarvavid huṃ hūṃ. The mantra of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Ratnasaṃbhava is:
Oṃ sarvavid traṃ trāṭ. The mantra of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Padma is:
Oṃ sarvavid huṃ. The mantra of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-karma is: Oṃ sarvavid aḥ aḥ.
The mantra of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-prabhāsa is: [Oṃ sarvavid aḥ aḥ].
Oṃ sarvavid. Oṃ oṃ. The mantra of the Ratnaketu-uṣṇīṣa is:
Oṃ sarvavid hūṃ hūṃ. The mantra of the Vajrāyudha-uṣṇīṣa is: Oṃ sarvavid hūṃ hūṃ.
Oṃ sarvavid huṃ ti phaṭ. This is the mantra of the White Parasol Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
Oṃ sarvavid kili phaṭ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Hāritī.
Oṃ sarvavid bhañja mahāvajranṛtyavajra nādaparāmita pūjaya hūṃ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Mālā.
Oṃ sarvavid bho mahāvajranṛpa śīlaparāmitāpūjite traṃ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Gopa.
Oṃ sarvavid bhaṭa mahāvajrotpāta kṣāntiparāmitāpūjye hrīḥ. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Vajra is as follows:
Oṃ sarvavid bhagavan vīreśvara parameśvara āḥ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin.
Oṃ sarvavidbhaḥ sarvapāpaviśodhani dharmadharmas tūṣṇīmbhāvanapratipatti hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the Flower Bodhisattva.
Oṃ sarvavid buddha-sarvanirgatisthodani kṛiṣṇaparikṛiṣṭacchedanani puṣpavilokini prajñāprabhāmita-bhujye traṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Dīpa.
Oṃ sarvavidbhaḥ sarvapāpaviśodhani jñānālokakari pratinidhipramiti-bhuje hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Gandhapuṣpā.
Oṃ sarvavid puṣpābhyo gandha-nivedani vajra-gandha-prayāmita-pūjaye hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśī.
Oṃ sarvavidbhanāragagataye āgariṣṇi hūṃ jaḥ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa.
Oṃ sarvavid bhaḥ sarvanaraka-uddhāraṇī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Vajrasaṃkalā.
Oṃ sarvavid puṣpābhyām̐dhana mocani hūṃ vaṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Vajraghaṇṭā.
Oṃ sarvavidbhaḥ sarvapāyaga tigahanaviśodhani hūṃ hoḥ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the Great Bodhisattva; the mantra of Maitreya Bodhisattva is as follows:
Oṃ maigharaṇāya svāhā. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin is:
Oṃ amoghe amoghapāśe hūṃ. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Sarvapāpavināśana is: [Oṃ sarvapāpavināśane hūṃ].
Oṃ sarvavyādhahara sarvavyādhiśodhani hūṃ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Sarvaduḥkhapraśamanī (Destroyer of All Sorrow and Darkness).
Oṃ sarvaśukladharmānirghātana-mati hūṃ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin.
Oṃ khaṇḍahastini hūṃ. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Vīra is: Oṃ śūraṅgami hūṃ.
The mantra of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha is: [Oṃ ākāśagarbhe hūṃ].
Oṃ gāgani gaganalocani hūṃ. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu is:
Oṃ jñānaketo jñānavati hūṃ. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Amṛtaprabha is:
Oṃ amṛta-pravī āmṛta-vati hūṃ. This is the mantra of Candraprabha Bodhisattva.
Oṃ jñāna-stite jñāna-māvalokite svāhā. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla.
Oṃ vāradravati vārapāri hūṃ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Jvalanaprabha.
Oṃ jvalini mahājvalini hūṃ. This is the mantra of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
Oṃ vajragarve hūṃ. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati is:
Oṃ akṣaye phaṭ. Akṣayakarmavāraṇa viśodhani svāhā. The mantra of the Bodhisattva Pratisamvitkūṭa is:
Oṃ pratibhāne mahāpratibhāne pratibhānakoṭi svāhā. This is the mantra of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Oṃ samantavajri hūṃ. Whenever an ācārya wishes to recite such subtle mantras of the Buddhas and great bodhisattvas, [he should do so].
Having visualized the noble deities through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) associated with the three types of arising,
and once they have appeared before one, one should then perform the mudrā for opening the gate.
This mudrā is formed by making vajra-fists with both hands.
Extend the two index fingers and hook the two little fingers together like a lock;
then recite the mantra for opening the gate as follows:
Oṃ sarvavid bīja-vajra-nodana-ghātaya hūṃ. Having recited this mantra, [proceed].
Then, perform the gesture of drawing back the hands as if opening a lock.
Next, form the Vajra Dharma Seal:
with both hands, make the vajra-bind (*vajrabandha*).
Again, change the left hand to perform the finger-snap gesture.
While forming this mudrā,
visualize Śākyamuni Buddha reciting the mantra from his own mouth:
Oṃ sarvavidvaja hūṃ. Having performed it thus, recite as desired.
Furthermore, the Ācārya, as previously practiced,
visualizes the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the maṇḍala,
together with their respective physical forms, mantras, and mudrās.
Regarding the various phenomena such as emanations and so forth,
one must perform the visualization at each of the three periods of the day.
Once the visualization has been successfully accomplished, [one may proceed].
Only then may one direct the mind to perform various practices.
In this manner, for one month, three months, or even up to six months,
one should cultivate these preliminary practices until they are thoroughly mastered.
Furthermore, one should pray for the majestic empowerment and protection of the Buddhas and noble sages to manifest auspicious signs;
once such auspiciousness has been attained,
one may then begin by selecting a site and constructing the maṇḍala.
And [the painting of] powdered images of the noble ones and so forth.
Furthermore, when an ācārya wishes to establish a maṇḍala,
he must select an excellent site, such as a temple or dwelling.
Whether in a village, a grove, or similar locations,
if one obtains ground where a boundary has previously been established, there is no need for further consecration; however,
if it is ground that has not been consecrated, one should dig down to the depth of the neck.
It may reach the navel or the knees.
The ācārya gazes directly at it;
if there are ashes, charcoal, husks, bones, or even particles of sand and stone.
All [impurities] should be completely removed.
Then, using separate, fragrant, pure, and excellent soil, fill [the area] until it is level and even.
The Ācārya should recite the mantras of the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā, Vajrayakṣa, and Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
Having sprinkled consecrated water to purify the ground,
the ācārya then enters the vajra-expulsion-of-māras samādhi at that very spot.
Furthermore, one should visualize that from within the heart-mantra,
the Great Wrathful Vidyārāja is born,
his two eyes like the sun and moon.
Holding a *karmavajra* with blazing, radiant flames,
he performs the vajra-stride and gazes to the left and right;
in a single *kṣaṇa*, he is able to subdue all māras.
The ācārya then holds a bell in his left hand and a vajra in his right hand,
and performs the vajra-walk upon the site of the maṇḍala.
Extending even to the Vajra-perimeter,
one should again bind the root mudrā,
recite the mantra for expelling māras, and utter the syllable HŪṂ.
Performing the dance gestures as described above and assuming the sovereign form of a Vidyārāja,
circumambulate that site while reciting the mantra to dispatch all māras.
The mantra is:
Oṃ vajra-ghaṭṭa-kīli kīlaya sarvavighnān bandha hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this Vajrakīla mantra twice.
The mantra for nailing the ritual stake into the ground is as follows:
Oṃ kṣe kṣe gata-gata sarva-duṣṭān phaṭ kīlaya kīlaya sarva-bhūtān phaṭ vajra-kīla vajra-dāruṇiya āvartaya svāhā. The Ācārya then constructs the maṇḍala.
Having selected a superior site,
one should first determine the dimensions of the intended structure according to its scale.
If it is for a king, it should be made one hundred cubits or fifty cubits in size.
If for a high minister or even a commoner,
it may be made twenty-five cubits or twelve cubits;
if one lacks the means, it may be made one cubit.
Having measured it in this manner,
one then applies cow dung to coat it completely,
and further sprinkles it with consecrated five-fold pure water (*pañcagavya*).
Furthermore, having finished adorning [the image] by applying scented unguents,
the ācārya shall then bathe until pure,
anoint his body with fragrance, put on fresh garments, and wear a jeweled crown upon his head.
Once the site has been adorned and purified with flower garlands,
one should first perform a homa sacrifice upon the maṇḍala ground using moist wood that has thorns,
measuring eight finger-widths in length and having eight facets.
Furthermore, one should use poisons, mustard seeds, human blood,
powdered bone, and so forth, mixed with pungent oils;
these are burned together with damp firewood as a homa offering.
Making the finger-snapping gesture with the right hand, recite the mantra:
Oṃ sarvavid-vajra-samāja jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ. Once this has been accomplished, there is no need for further ritual decoration of the consecrated site.
Then, first on that ground,
one should measure out an area as wide as a single hide and smear it with cow dung.
Above that, according to the ritual procedure,
one should place five *kalaśas* (vases) and perform the *homa* rite using moist fuel and yellow pine wood, twelve finger-widths in length.
Having first performed the homa with black sesame, barley, wheat, non-glutinous rice, and ghee,
one addresses the Earth Deity, saying:
"I now [perform this] for the sake of a king, a minister, or even a disciple and their retinue."
Construct a maṇḍala upon this ground.
For the sake of benefiting us, you earth-dwelling deities, arouse a heart of compassion and perform virtuous deeds for my sake.
Having performed the homa in this manner, one will be able to accomplish all matters.
Then the ācārya, together with his assistants,
takes the thread and measures out the maṇḍala;
the thread shall be of five colors.
Soak [the object] overnight in scented water.
Then, place it in a golden vessel and,
holding it with both hands, recite the mantra of the Five Buddha-Uṣṇīṣas.
Having performed the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one offers it to the five Buddhas.
Then, one requests this thread back from the five Buddhas, saying:
"May the Buddhas, out of their great compassion, grant it to me together."
Immediately, he combined all five colors into one and recited this gāthā:
"Distinguishing all phenomena, they now truly encompass one another."
The ultimate reality is non-dual; this thread is likewise so.
Furthermore, having combined the measurements of the length and breadth of this thread according to the dimensions of the maṇḍala, it is fully completed.
Then, reciting the mantra, he empowers the thread with this mantra:
Oṃ vajrasūtradhāra maṇḍale hūṃ. Having thus empowered the thread, the ācārya—
Then, together with his companions, he stood at the southwest corner of the maṇḍala and recited the mantra:
Oṃ vajrasūtradhāra mārgiśaya mardikrama hūṃ. Having recited the mantra, [he proceeded].
The Ācārya holds one end of the cord and proceeds facing east,
standing at the southeast corner.
His assistant holds the other end of the cord and proceeds toward the north.
Having stood at the northwest corner and completed the marking lines,
next the ācārya proceeds northward to the northeast corner, while his assistant proceeds southward to the southwest corner.
The marking lines are thus drawn, encircling the four directions.
The second and third tiers follow this same sequence.
If the marking lines are performed according to the ritual rules, it is called the "complete maṇḍala."
If one does not act according to the ritual,
both the ācārya and his assistants will incur faults.
The maṇḍala has four sides and four gates.
Each gate has a pavilion.
Upon these gate-pavilions, one should paint the sun and moon, as well as jewel necklaces, decorating them according to one's preference.
In the center, one should paint an eight-spoked wheel.
Outside the wheel, draw a vajra perimeter.
First, in the center of the wheel, draw Śākyamuni Buddha.
On the spoke in the eastern position, draw the Tathāgata Vajramahāuṣṇīṣa.
On the spoke in the southern position, paint the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Ratnasaṃbhava; on the spoke in the western position, paint the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Padma;
and on the spoke in the northern position, paint the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Karma.
Having thus painted these four Tathāgatas, [proceed as follows].
Next, in the southeast corner, draw the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Prabhāsa;
in the southwest corner, draw the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Ratnaketu;
and in the northwest corner, draw the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Vajratīkṣṇa.
In the northeast corner, one should paint the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa;
thus, having painted the eight Tathāgatas upon the eight spokes of the wheel.
Next, in the four corners of the wheel, paint the four attendant bodhisattvas.
In the four corners of the second tier, paint the four bodhisattvas of garlands, dance, and song.
In the four corners of the third tier...
Paint the four Bodhisattvas of Incense, Flower, Lamp, and Ointment;
at the four gates, paint the four Gate-protecting Bodhisattvas;
and next, in the four directions, paint the sixteen Great Bodhisattvas.
Outside each of the four gates, on both sides of the lintel,
paint elephants and lions;
on both sides of each gate, paint the eight auspicious symbols.
Within the mountain enclosure, draw the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
In the east, draw Śakra;
his right hand holds a vajra, and his left hand rests at his hip.
He rides upon a six-tusked white elephant,
with two celestial maidens depicted on either side:
the first named Śeṣī and the second named Ulūpī.
In the southeast, one should paint the deity Agni.
His body is red in color, with blazing and intense radiance.
His right hand holds a *kamaṇḍalu*, and his left hand holds a jeweled staff.
He rides a red-colored ram.
In the south, one should paint Yāma Heaven;
his body is green in color.
The left hand forms a fist placed at the side of the waist;
the right hand holds a jeweled staff;
he rides upon a water buffalo.
On both sides, depict images of the gods of the central realm.
In the southwest, depict the Lord of the Rākṣasas,
his body dark red in color, with radiance like a mass of fire.
Holding a sword in his right hand and resting his left hand at his hip,
he sits upon a ghost.
To the west, one should paint Varuṇa.
His body is yellowish-white in color, with the head of a nāga appearing upon his crown.
His right hand holds a noose, and his left hand holds a wondrous jewel.
He rides upon a red makara fish.
On both sides, paint the nāga goddesses and their retinues;
in the northwest corner, paint the Wind Deity (Vāyu),
whose body is the color of space.
Holding a banner and riding upon a deer,
in the north is painted the Lord of Yakṣas,
his body golden in color.
His right hand grasps a branch of a precious tree and his left hand holds a precious casket;
he rides upon a white horse,
with yakṣiṇīs depicted on both sides.
In the northeastern corner, paint the Lord of Bhūtas;
his body is ash-gray in color.
His right hand holds a trident, and his left hand holds a *kamaṇḍalu* filled with *vajra*-seeds.
Mounted upon a yellow ox,
he is positioned below the front of the maṇḍala; there,
one should draw the Earth Deity (Pṛthivī).
His body is golden in color.
With both hands at his chest, he holds a vase of nectar.
He sits upon a lotus seat.
On the right side, paint an asura with a body of reddish-black hue,
clad in armor and holding a sharp sword in hand, riding upon the *kulika* nāga.
On the left side, paint the Great Nāga King;
his body is white, and he sits upon his original seat,
holding a precious vessel filled with various jewels.
And paint two nāga girls,
their bodies yellow in color and possessing marks of exquisite beauty;
they hold the Prajñāpāramitā sūtra, a rosary, a water jar (kamaṇḍalu), and display the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā).
Above the front of the maṇḍala,
draw a sun disk on the left and a full moon on the right.
Outside the mountain range, in the southeast corner:
Depict the eight hells, beginning with Avīci;
in the southwest corner, depict the realm of hungry ghosts (preta);
and in the northwest corner, depict the various realms of animals (tiryagyoni).
In the northeast corner, one should paint the human realm.
Having painted thus,
the ācārya [enters] into the maṇḍala.
Offer kumuda incense, various types of incense, flowers, food, drink, and so forth.
Furthermore, take a full *argha* vessel filled with scented water and empower it by reciting the Vajrayakṣa mantra.
As for the various articles used in the maṇḍala,
having consecrated each with its respective root mantra,
one should offer them to all the noble deities, causing them all to be fully delighted.
Furthermore, having empowered the maṇḍala with the Vajrayakṣa mantra,
one should then recite the syllable HŪṂ four times.
Having removed the boundary-marking vajra-kīlas,
one should immediately fill [the area] with five-colored powders, cultivating it until it is level and even.
Thereafter, the ācārya begins from the northeast corner.
Using five-colored powders, one should fashion the images of the various Buddhas and holy sages.
When applying the powders, they should follow the sequence of white, blue, red, and green;
for the center, yellow is used to form an eight-spoked wheel.
The eastern direction is pure white;
the southern direction is deep blue;
the western direction is red.
The northern direction is green.
Having thus completed the powdering of the images of the noble ones,
the ācārya again visualizes the space maṇḍala as before.
First, form the firm upward-facing gesture with the two vajra-fingers of both hands and visualize the mantra arising as the space-maṇḍala. Then,
as before, visualize them merging into one to become the ultimate reality.
The maṇḍala having been completed,
one should then construct a separate small platform outside the southern gate of the maṇḍala.
The area on all four sides should be approximately one cubit in width;
smear it with cow dung that does not fall to the ground,
and afterwards, purify it by sprinkling the five kinds of pure water.
Furthermore, using white sandalwood incense,
one should draw a maṇḍala at the center of the platform in the shape of a full moon.
Above, one should present various offerings such as incense, flowers, food, and drink,
up to the "arising" [mantra] and so forth;
furthermore, one should spread out blue *śara* grass.
Upon it, place an *argha* vase filled with the five jewels, the five grains, and the five medicines,
and insert various flowers, fruits, tree branches, and leaves.
Tie a blue cloth around the neck of the vase.
Nevertheless, empower it with the root mantra and make the aspiration that this water shall bring great benefit.
Furthermore, recite the root mantra to empower white mustard seeds, white flowers, and so forth.
Reciting the mantra orally,
one strikes a person, or the name of a person, or their clothing, and so forth, with white mustard seeds and white flowers.
Furthermore, by sprinkling argha water,
all such performed acts— whether for pacifying calamities, increasing prosperity, or other purposes— will yield immeasurable and boundless merit;
this extends even to striking the bones or reciting the names of deceased persons.
The mantra for causing the deceased to depart from all evil realms and be reborn in the celestial worlds is as follows:
Oṃ sarvabāpanāhana vajra hūṃ phaṭ. Oṃ sarvabāpaviśodhana.
VAJRA HŪṂ PHAṬ | OṂ SARVA KARMĀVARAṆANI VASMI KRODHA HŪṂ PHAṬ | OṂ BHRŪṂ VINĀŚAYA ||
Varaṇani hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ turaṅgaviśuddhe varaṇani hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ jvala jvala dagha dagha hana hana ||
1. Āvaranani hūṃ phaṭ. 2. Oṃ suloma sara sara prasara prasara āvaraṇani hūṃ phaṭ. 3. Oṃ hūṃ hara.
Hara sarvavāraṇani hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ sarvāvaraṇani sphoṭaya hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ bhrīḥ ||
Vajratuṇḍa hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ traṭ traṭ sarvāvaraṇani hūṃ traḥ ||
1. RAṬ ṢVĀUM 2. OṂ CINA CINĀ VIṆARA VA VIṆARA VA 3.
SARVA-ĀVARAṆANI 4. HŪṂ PHAṬ 5. OṂ NAHA NAHA SARVA-ĀVARAṆĀNI SVĀHĀ.
Naraka-gati-he-dūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ paca paca sarvabhūtānāṃ gati he dūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ matha matha sarva... ||
Recite *ṭiriya-gati-hiṃ ṭoṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Then, again recite the mantra for washing away karmic obstacles.
While reciting the mantra:
Previously, one sprinkles water from an *argha* vessel to accomplish the purification of karmic obscurations.
The mantra is as follows:

Oṃ namo bhagavate sarva-nirgatipariśodhana-rājāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya | tadyathā | śodhani śodhani | sarvapāpaviśodhani | jati vijati | sarvakarmāvaraṇa-vijati | svāhā || Having recited this mantra, [one performs the sprinkling].
If it is for the deceased,
one should further recite for them mantras such as those for rebirth in a pure land and the path of purity.
If it is for the purpose of increasing auspiciousness or performing an empowerment, [one should likewise do so].
Thus, one does not employ it.
The mantra for rebirth in the Pure Land is:
Oṃ ratne ratne ratnasambhave ratnagiri ratnamālavati śuddhaye sarvapāpaṃ hūṃ traṭ. The mantra for the pure path is:
Oṃ paṭme paṭme paṭmopavi sukhāvatyagaccha svāhā. Thirdly, construct the maṇḍala as described above and perform the recitation.
When seeking matters such as pacification, increase, and auspiciousness,
one must perform [the rites] three times each day with incense,
flowers, and various kinds of offerings.
Having made offerings to the Buddhas and noble sages of the maṇḍala,
and having offered auspicious praises and hymns of praise to the Buddhas and noble sages,
one should do so with single-minded devotion and without slackening for three days, five days, or eight days.
While performing the homa to seek various aspirations,
if one is to bestow empowerment upon a disciple,
one should immediately place it within the consecrated añjali-vessel (kalaśa).
Draw white lotus flowers upon the ground.
Within each flower, draw an eight-spoked wheel.
In the center of each wheel, place a white *argha* vase.
Fill a flask with various substances such as the five jewels and the five medicines to create consecrated water (*prokṣaṇī*).
Having further empowered it with the root mantra,
one should then lead the disciple into the maṇḍala according to the ritual procedure.
Having conferred the empowerment and bestowed the sublime Dharma, and so forth,
one should perform the visualization of union according to the ritual procedure,
contemplating all sentient beings in the evil destinies within saṃsāra.
They all obtain purification through bathing, whereby their karmic obscurations are extinguished;
they achieve a body of merit and are reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven or the Tuṣita Heaven.
Next, the *argha* vase is explained.
It should be covered with white cloth;
the vessel, which has long lips, a large neck, and a full belly,
should be filled with scented water and adorned with various flowers, fruits, and branches of trees.
Furthermore, fill [the vases] with the five precious substances, the five medicinal herbs, the five grains, and so forth.
Spread out *śara* grass (green auspicious grass) and place the vases upon it.
Tie a blue cloth around the neck of each vase; this is the ritual method for the vases.
If one performs homa,
one should place the vases accordingly at the eastern gate of the maṇḍala,
and hang white parasols, flower garlands, and so forth above them.
Furthermore, five-headed banners should be set up on the four sides.
In front, construct a homa fire-pit;
it should be two cubits wide at the top and one cubit at the bottom.
The heights and depths, the colors and insignia,
all strictly follow the rules of the Fundamental Mahāyāna Dharma;
for the homa ritual, one must use *guggulu* incense.
Dragon-flower auspicious fruits and various other fruits;
black sesame, barley, and wheat;
cooked rice, clarified butter, honey, curd, milk, and moist firewood, and so forth.
When all these articles have been fully prepared,
the ācārya holds the vajra and bell in his hands and presses them upon each of the objects,
consecrating each with its respective root mantra one hundred and eight times.
The ritual for consecrating the image and performing the celebration is also conducted according to this same procedure.
All materials required for the homa should be placed to the right of the homa hearth.
Place only the alms bowl to the left of the hearth.
The ācārya should perform the visualization corresponding to the three signs according to the ritual rules,
and then sprinkle the hearth with pure water.
Having performed the ritual sprinkling for purification,
one shall kindle a fire within the hearth;
once the fire has become blazing, [proceed].
Furthermore, one sprinkles the flames lightly with *argha* water.
Then, the *ācārya*, having bound the mudrā and recited the mantra,
performs the invocation while visualizing that the Fire Deity appears within the fire.
Then, with ghee, honey, curd, and substances to be offered to the Fire God,
one should cast them into the fire three times while reciting the mantra to present them to the Fire God.
Thereafter, one should bind the Vajracakra-mudrā.
Form vajra-fists with both hands,
then modify them into the vajra-bind to complete the seal.
And recite the Vajracakra mantra as follows:
Oṃ sarvavid vajrakīlite hūṃ vaśya vajrasamayi vajracaṭa vimokṣaya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ. While forming the mudrā, recite the mantra with the appropriate intonation for *jaḥ*.
One should visualize the maṇḍala appearing within the hearth;
all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy sages will then manifest before one.
The ācārya should then direct his mind with utmost devotion.
One should prepare one hundred and eight *srūva* offerings using various *homa* substances;
if using only clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one should simply cast seven *srūva*.
In this manner, one makes offerings to all the Buddhas and noble sages (*ārya*).
Furthermore, one performs the eight offerings, such as playful garlands, song, and dance,
up to the twenty-five kinds of offerings.
The ācārya thus performs the various rites of visualization, maṇḍala, and homa.
Whether for kings, ministers, commoners, disciples, or others,
one should benefit sentient beings according to their specific requests;
even those who merely rejoice upon seeing or hearing [this practice] shall all obtain immeasurable merit.
